rd-school-c12-accountancy-b.share-capita.title: Accounting for Share Capital
rd-school-c12-accountancy-b.share-capita.subtitle: How a company raises money from thousands of owners — and how every rupee is recorded

sections.h: Owning a sliver of a giant
sections.md:
When Priya, a 19-year-old in Indore, buys a few shares of a listed company through her banking app, she becomes one of its owners. So do lakhs of others. No partnership deed could ever hold so many people — and that is precisely why the **company** form exists.

A **company** is an artificial person created by law. The Companies Act, 2013 defines it simply as a company incorporated under that Act or an earlier company law. Its **features**:
- **Body corporate / separate legal entity** — it can own property, sue and be sued in its own name, distinct from its members.
- **Perpetual succession** — members may come and go, but the company continues.
- **Limited liability** — a member's liability is limited to the unpaid amount on shares held.
- **Transferability of shares** — shares of a public company are freely transferable.
- **Common seal** — once the company's official signature; now optional, documents may be signed by authorised directors.
- **Separation of ownership and management** — shareholders own, an elected board of directors manages.
- **May sue and be sued** in its own name.

Its capital is divided into small units called **shares**.

This chapter, in textbook order:

1. Features and kinds of companies
2. Share and share capital — categories
3. Types of shares (equity and preference)
4. Issue of shares — public issue, private placement, ESOPs, sweat equity
5. Accounting for issue at par and at premium; for cash and for consideration other than cash
6. Under-subscription, over-subscription and pro-rata allotment
7. Calls in arrears and calls in advance
8. Forfeiture and re-issue of forfeited shares
9. Disclosure of share capital in the Balance Sheet

> Did you know? Under the Companies Act, 2013 (Section 53), shares cannot be issued at a discount except **sweat equity** shares — so this chapter focuses on issue at par and at premium.
keyTerms: Separate legal entity — company is distinct from its members
Perpetual succession — company continues regardless of changes in members
Limited liability — members lose at most the unpaid amount on their shares

check.q: Which feature means a company continues to exist even if all its shareholders change?
check.why: Perpetual succession means the company's life is unaffected by death, insolvency or exit of its members.

sections.md:
**On the basis of liability:**
- *Company limited by shares* — liability limited to unpaid amount on shares (the most common).
- *Company limited by guarantee* — members guarantee to contribute a fixed sum on winding up (often clubs, charities).
- *Unlimited company* — members' liability is unlimited.

**On the basis of members:**
- **Private company** — minimum 2, maximum 200 members (excluding employee-members); restricts the right to transfer shares; cannot invite the public to subscribe. Name ends with 'Private Limited'.
- **Public company** — minimum 7 members, no maximum; shares freely transferable; may invite the public. A private company that is a subsidiary of a public company is treated as public.
- **One Person Company (OPC)** — a single natural person as member, a nominee named in the memorandum.

**Other categories:** *government company* (at least 51% paid-up capital held by Central/State governments), *holding and subsidiary companies*, *listed companies* (securities listed on a recognised stock exchange such as NSE or BSE), *associate companies*.

check.q: The maximum number of members in a private company (excluding employees) is:
check.why: The Companies Act, 2013 caps a private company at 200 members, excluding present and past employee-members.

sections.h: Share and categories of share capital
sections.md:
A **share** is the smallest unit into which a company's capital is divided — for example, capital of ₹10 lakh in 1,00,000 shares of ₹10 each. The ₹10 is the **nominal or face value**.

**Share capital categories**, like nested boxes:

| Category | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Authorised (registered/nominal) capital | Maximum the Memorandum of Association allows; can be raised by following the procedure |
| Issued capital | Part of authorised capital offered for subscription (including shares to vendors) |
| Subscribed capital | Part of issued capital actually taken up by the public |
| Called-up capital | Part of subscribed capital the company has asked to be paid |
| Paid-up capital | Part of called-up actually received (called-up − calls in arrears) |
| Uncalled capital | Subscribed but not yet called |
| Reserve capital | Uncalled capital to be called only on winding up (by special resolution) |

Subscribed capital is further split into **subscribed and fully paid** and **subscribed but not fully paid** in the notes to accounts.

*Example:* Authorised ₹10,00,000; issued 60,000 shares of ₹10; subscribed 55,000; ₹8 per share called; calls of ₹4,000 unpaid. Called-up = 55,000 × 8 = 4,40,000. Paid-up = 4,36,000. Uncalled = 55,000 × 2 = 1,10,000.

check.q: The part of subscribed capital which the company has asked shareholders to pay is:
check.why: Called-up capital is the portion of the face value of subscribed shares the company has demanded so far.

sections.md:
Section 43 of the Companies Act, 2013 allows only two kinds of share capital.

**Preference shares** carry two preferential rights: (i) dividend at a **fixed rate** before equity shareholders, and (ii) return of capital before equity on winding up. Varieties:
- *Cumulative* (unpaid dividend accumulates as arrears) vs *non-cumulative*.
- *Participating* (share surplus profits with equity after a fixed dividend) vs *non-participating*.
- *Convertible* (into equity after a period) vs *non-convertible*.
- *Redeemable* — repayable after a fixed period. Since 2013, Indian companies cannot issue **irredeemable** preference shares; the maximum life is normally 20 years.

**Equity shares** are all shares that are not preference shares. They carry voting rights, bear the most risk, and enjoy residual profits — dividends vary with profits. Equity may be *with voting rights* or *with differential rights* as to dividend or voting.

| Point | Preference | Equity |
|---|---|---|
| Dividend | Fixed rate, paid first | Variable, paid after preference |
| Capital on winding up | Returned first | Returned last |
| Voting | Limited to matters affecting them | Full |
| Risk | Lower | Higher |
| Redemption | Redeemable | Not redeemable (except buy-back) |

check.q: Which right is NOT normally available to preference shareholders?
options: Full voting rights in all matters
check.why: Preference shareholders generally vote only on matters directly affecting them, not on all matters.

sections.h: How shares are issued: public issue, private placement, ESOP, sweat equity
sections.md:
**Public issue (the classic route).** The company issues a **prospectus** inviting the public. Investors fill in an application form and pay **application money** — by law at least 5% of nominal value (SEBI requires at least 25% of issue price for public issues). Money is kept in a separate scheduled bank account until allotment. The company can allot only if it receives the **minimum subscription** — 90% of the issue — within the stipulated period; otherwise all money must be refunded. After allotment it collects **allotment money**, and later the balance in one or more **calls** (first call, second and final call). Under Table F, no call may exceed 25% of nominal value, with at least one month between calls.

**Private placement** — offering shares to a select group of persons (not more than 200 in a financial year, excluding qualified institutional buyers and employees under ESOP), through a private placement offer letter. It is quicker and cheaper than a public issue.

**Employees Stock Option Plan (ESOP)** — the option given to directors, officers and employees to buy the company's shares at a future date at a pre-determined (usually lower) price, to reward and retain them.

**Sweat equity shares** — issued at a discount or for consideration other than cash to employees or directors for providing know-how, intellectual property or value additions.

> Did you know? Today almost all public issues in India are made through **ASBA** (Application Supported by Blocked Amount) — your money stays in your bank account, merely blocked, until allotment. UPI is also used to block funds.

check.q: Minimum subscription that must be received before allotment is:
check.why: The law requires at least 90% of the issued amount to be subscribed, or all application money must be refunded.

sections.h: Issue of shares at par and at premium
sections.md:
**At par:** issue price = face value. **At premium:** issue price > face value; premium is credited to **Securities Premium A/c**, usable only for purposes in Section 52: issuing fully paid bonus shares, writing off preliminary expenses, writing off expenses/commission/discount on issue of shares or debentures, providing for premium payable on redemption of preference shares or debentures, and buy-back of own shares. Premium is shown under Reserves and Surplus.

**Journal entries (shares issued payable in instalments):**

1. Application money received: Bank Dr. To Share Application A/c
2. Application transferred: Share Application Dr. To Share Capital (and To Securities Premium, if premium collected with application)
3. Allotment due: Share Allotment Dr. To Share Capital, To Securities Premium
4. Allotment received: Bank Dr. To Share Allotment
5. Call due: Share First Call Dr. To Share Capital
6. Call received: Bank Dr. To Share First Call

Some companies use a single **Share Application and Allotment A/c** when both are paid together.

**Example:** Narmada Ltd issues 10,000 equity shares of ₹10 each at ₹12. Payable: ₹3 on application, ₹5 on allotment (including ₹2 premium), ₹4 on first and final call. All money received.

- Application: 30,000 → Share Capital 30,000
- Allotment: 50,000 → Share Capital 30,000 + Securities Premium 20,000
- Call: 40,000 → Share Capital 40,000

Total capital = 30,000 + 30,000 + 40,000 = ₹1,00,000 = 10,000 × 10 ✓. Premium ₹20,000 ✓. Total cash ₹1,20,000 ✓.

**Under-subscription** — fewer shares applied for than offered. If at least the minimum subscription is received, the company simply allots the shares applied for; capital is recorded only for shares allotted.

check.q: Which of these is NOT a permitted use of securities premium?
check.why: Securities premium is a capital receipt and cannot be distributed as dividend; Section 52 lists only specific capital uses.

sections.h: Issue for consideration other than cash
sections.md:
A company may acquire assets — land, machinery or a whole business — from a **vendor** and pay by issuing shares, at par or premium. Shares may also be issued to **promoters** for their services in forming the company.

**Entries:**
1. Sundry Assets Dr. To Sundry Liabilities, To Vendor (Goodwill Dr if consideration exceeds net assets; Capital Reserve Cr if less).
2. Vendor Dr. To Share Capital, To Securities Premium.

For promoters: Incorporation Costs (or Goodwill) Dr. To Share Capital.

**Number of shares = purchase consideration ÷ issue price.**

*Example:* Machinery ₹2,40,000 paid by equity shares of ₹10 at ₹12 → 20,000 shares; Share Capital 2,00,000; Securities Premium 40,000.

*Example with fraction:* Consideration ₹1,00,000 paid in ₹10 shares at ₹11 → 9,090.9 shares. Issue 9,090 shares (₹99,990) and pay ₹10 in cash.

check.q: A company buys machinery for ₹2,40,000 and pays by issuing equity shares of ₹10 each at ₹12. Number of shares issued:
check.why: Number of shares equals 2,40,000 ÷ ₹12 issue price, which is 20,000 shares.

sections.md:
Popular issues receive more applications than shares offered. The company can: (a) reject some applications and refund money, (b) allot **pro-rata** (proportionately), or (c) a combination — reject some, allot pro-rata to the rest.

In pro-rata allotment, **excess application money** is adjusted towards allotment (and, if the articles allow, towards calls); any surplus beyond that is refunded.

**Example:** Shares offered 10,000. Applications 15,000. Application ₹3, allotment ₹5. All applicants receive shares pro-rata (10,000 : 15,000 = 2 : 3).

- Application money received = 15,000 × 3 = ₹45,000
- Needed for application on 10,000 shares = ₹30,000
- Excess = ₹15,000
- Allotment due = 10,000 × 5 = ₹50,000
- Excess adjusted to allotment: ₹15,000 → cash due on allotment ₹35,000

Entry for application: Share Application Dr 45,000 To Share Capital 30,000, To Share Allotment 15,000.

**Tricky case — a defaulting pro-rata allottee.** Mohan applied for 600 shares and got 400 (ratio 2:3). He paid ₹1,800 on application; ₹1,200 was needed, so ₹600 excess went to allotment. Allotment due on his shares = 400 × 5 = 2,000, so he owed ₹1,400 and failed to pay. If his shares are forfeited, the amount *received* on them = application 1,800 (i.e. 1,200 + 600 adjusted).

check.why: Applicants who are rejected receive no shares, so their application money must be refunded.

sections.h: Calls in arrears and calls in advance
sections.md:
**Calls in arrears** — amount called (on allotment or calls) but not paid by the due date. Two ways to record:
1. Leave the unpaid balance in the Allotment/Call A/c; or
2. Open a **Calls-in-Arrears A/c**: Calls-in-Arrears Dr. To Share First Call.

In the Balance Sheet notes, calls in arrears are **deducted** from subscribed capital (under 'subscribed but not fully paid'). If the articles allow, the company may charge interest (Table F: up to **10% p.a.**): Shareholders Dr To Interest on Calls in Arrears; Bank Dr To Shareholders.

**Calls in advance** — money received before it is called. Entry: Bank Dr. To Calls-in-Advance A/c. When the call is later made, Calls-in-Advance Dr. To Share Call. It is a **liability** (shown under Other Current Liabilities), not part of share capital, and the company must pay interest if the articles provide (Table F: up to **12% p.a.**): Interest on Calls in Advance Dr To Shareholders; Shareholders Dr To Bank.

*Example:* Holder of 1,000 shares pays the final call of ₹3 along with allotment. Calls in advance = ₹3,000. If the call is made 6 months later, interest at 12% = 3,000 × 12% × 6/12 = ₹180.

check.q: Interest on calls in advance under Table F can be paid at a maximum of:
check.why: Table F of the Companies Act, 2013 allows interest on calls in advance at up to 12% per annum.

sections.md:
If a shareholder fails to pay allotment or call money, the directors may, after giving at least 14 days' notice, **forfeit** the shares — cancel them and keep whatever has been paid. The shareholder ceases to be a member.

**Entry on forfeiture:**

> Share Capital A/c Dr. (called-up amount on those shares)
> Securities Premium A/c Dr. (only if premium was called but not received)
> To Share Allotment/Calls A/c (unpaid amounts)
> To Share Forfeiture A/c (amount received)

If premium was already received, it is **not** debited — premium once received stays in Securities Premium.

**Example:** Ravi holds 200 shares of Narmada Ltd (₹10, issued at ₹12). He paid application only (₹3), failed allotment (₹5 incl. premium) and call (₹4). Shares forfeited.

> Share Capital Dr 2,000 (200 × 10)
> Securities Premium Dr 400 (200 × 2)
> To Share Allotment 1,000
> To Share First & Final Call 800
> To Share Forfeiture 600

Check: 2,400 = 2,400 ✓.

Share Forfeiture A/c is shown in the notes, added to subscribed capital, until the shares are re-issued.

check.q: On forfeiture of shares issued at premium, securities premium is debited only when:
check.why: Premium that has been received is a permanent capital receipt; only premium called but unpaid is cancelled on forfeiture.

sections.h: Re-issue of forfeited shares and disclosure
sections.md:
Forfeited shares may be re-issued at par, premium or discount. The **discount on re-issue cannot exceed the amount forfeited** on those shares (and is debited to Share Forfeiture A/c, not to a loss account).

Ravi's 200 shares re-issued at ₹8 per share fully paid:

> Bank Dr 1,600
> Share Forfeiture Dr 400
> To Share Capital 2,000

Balance in Share Forfeiture = 600 − 400 = ₹200 — a capital profit, transferred to **Capital Reserve**:

> Share Forfeiture Dr 200 To Capital Reserve 200

If re-issued at premium, the premium goes to Securities Premium and the entire forfeited amount becomes capital reserve.

**Only part re-issued?** Transfer to capital reserve only the gain on the shares re-issued; the forfeited amount on the shares not yet re-issued stays in Share Forfeiture. E.g. 300 shares forfeited with ₹4 each received (₹1,200); 200 re-issued at ₹9 → discount 200; gain on re-issued shares = (200 × 4) − 200 = 600 to capital reserve; ₹400 stays in forfeiture.

**Disclosure:** Balance Sheet → Equity and Liabilities → Shareholders' Funds → (a) Share Capital, with a Note:

| Note: Share Capital | ₹ |
|---|---|
| Authorised: 1,00,000 equity shares of ₹10 | 10,00,000 |
| Issued: 60,000 equity shares of ₹10 | 6,00,000 |
| Subscribed and fully paid: 54,000 shares of ₹10 | 5,40,000 |
| Subscribed but not fully paid: 1,000 shares of ₹10, ₹8 called | 8,000 |
| Less: calls in arrears | (500) |
| Add: Share Forfeiture | 300 |
| Total | 5,47,800 |

Securities Premium and Capital Reserve appear in the note on Reserves and Surplus.

check.q: 100 shares of ₹10 on which ₹6 was paid were forfeited and re-issued at ₹7 fully paid. Amount to capital reserve:
check.why: Forfeited ₹600 less discount on re-issue ₹300 (100 × ₹3) leaves ₹300 to capital reserve.

workedExamples.q: Those 300 shares are re-issued at ₹9 as fully paid. Capital reserve?

B Ltd Dr 5,50,000 To Share Capital 5,00,000, To Securities Premium 50,000.

summary: A company is an artificial person with separate entity, perpetual succession and limited liability.
Kinds: by liability (shares, guarantee, unlimited) and by members (private, public, OPC); also government, holding/subsidiary, listed.
Capital categories: authorised ⊇ issued ⊇ subscribed ⊇ called-up ⊇ paid-up; reserve capital is called only on winding up.
Only two kinds of shares: preference (fixed dividend, capital priority, redeemable) and equity (residual risk, full vote).
Routes: public issue (minimum subscription 90%), private placement, ESOP, sweat equity.
Shares may be issued at par or premium; issue at discount is not allowed except sweat equity.
Securities premium can be used only for purposes listed in Section 52.
Shares can be issued for consideration other than cash, e.g. to vendors or promoters.
Over-subscription: reject, pro-rata, or both; excess adjusted to allotment and calls; surplus refunded.
Calls in arrears: max interest 10% p.a.; calls in advance: liability, max interest 12% p.a. (Table F).
Forfeiture: debit capital called-up, credit unpaid calls and forfeiture with amount received; debit premium only if unpaid.
Discount on re-issue cannot exceed forfeited amount; gain on re-issued shares goes to capital reserve.
Share capital is shown under Shareholders' Funds with details in Notes to Accounts.

Shares given to employees/directors at discount for know-how or value addition

rd-school-c12-biology-a.ch01-sexual-repr.title: Sexual Reproduction in Flowering Plants
rd-school-c12-biology-a.ch01-sexual-repr.subtitle: How a mango tree, which cannot walk, still finds a partner — and why every fruit is a love letter to the next generation

sections.h: 1. The puzzle of the rooted parent
sections.md:
Stand under a neem tree in April and look up. Thousands of tiny cream flowers, a hum of bees, a dusting of yellow on the leaves. That tree will never take a single step in its life, yet it must combine its genes with another neem tree, possibly a kilometre away. How?

The answer is the **flower** — the most elaborate reproductive device evolution has built. Angiosperms (flowering plants) are the most successful land plants on Earth, with well over 2.5 lakh species, and almost all of them reproduce sexually through flowers.

This chapter follows one complete journey:

1. **Pre-fertilisation events** — making the flower, the male gametes (inside pollen) and the female gamete (inside the ovule).
2. **Pollination** — getting pollen to the right stigma.
3. **Double fertilisation** — the unique angiosperm trick where *two* fusions happen.
4. **Post-fertilisation events** — endosperm, embryo, seed and fruit.
5. **Special cases** — apomixis and polyembryony.

Humans have always cared about flowers. We offer marigolds in temples, weave jasmine into hair, and grow roses for Valentine's Day. But for the plant, a flower is not decoration — it is the stage on which the next generation is set up.

> **Did you know?** The decision to flower is controlled by hormones and environmental signals like day length. Long before a bud is visible, the shoot apex has already changed from making leaves to making floral parts.
keyTerms: Angiosperm — plant whose seeds are enclosed inside a fruit
Pre-fertilisation — all events before gametes fuse
Post-fertilisation — events after fusion: seed and fruit formation

sections.h: 2. The stamen, the anther and the making of pollen
sections.md:
A typical flower has four whorls: calyx (sepals), corolla (petals), **androecium** (stamens, the male part) and **gynoecium** (pistils/carpels, the female part).

Each **stamen** has a long stalk, the **filament**, topped by a two-lobed **anther**. A typical angiosperm anther is **bilobed** and each lobe has two thecae, so it is called **dithecous**. In cross-section the anther shows four **microsporangia** (pollen sacs), one at each corner — a tetragonal structure.

### Wall of the microsporangium (outside to inside)
| Layer | Role |
|---|---|
| Epidermis | Protection |
| Endothecium | Helps in dehiscence (opening) |
| Middle layers (1–3) | Protection, degenerate later |
| **Tapetum** | Innermost; nourishes developing pollen; cells often have more than one nucleus |

In the centre lies the **sporogenous tissue**: compactly arranged diploid cells. Each can become a **microspore mother cell (pollen mother cell, PMC)**.

### Microsporogenesis
Each PMC undergoes **meiosis** to form a cluster of four haploid cells — a **microspore tetrad**. As the anther matures and dries, the microspores separate and develop into **pollen grains**. So one PMC → 4 pollen grains.

### The pollen grain
Pollen grains are usually spherical, about 25–50 micrometres across. They have a two-layered wall:
- **Exine** — outer, tough, made of **sporopollenin**, one of the most resistant organic materials known. It survives high heat, strong acids and alkalis, and no enzyme known can break it. That is why pollen fossils last for millions of years. Gaps in the exine where sporopollenin is absent are **germ pores**.
- **Intine** — inner, thin, continuous, made of cellulose and pectin.

A mature pollen grain contains two cells: a large **vegetative cell** (with food reserves and an irregular nucleus) and a small **generative cell** floating in its cytoplasm. In over 60% of angiosperms pollen is shed at this **2-celled stage**; in the rest, the generative cell divides mitotically first, giving **two male gametes** (3-celled stage).

The pollen grain is the **male gametophyte**.

> **Did you know?** Pollen of Parthenium (carrot grass), which arrived in India as a contaminant with imported wheat, causes allergies and asthma in many people. On the brighter side, pollen tablets are sold as food supplements, and pollen can be stored for years at −196 °C in liquid nitrogen in **pollen banks** for crop breeding.

check.why: The tapetum is the innermost wall layer; its dense, often multinucleate cells feed the developing microspores.

sections.h: 3. The pistil, the ovule and the embryo sac
sections.md:
The **gynoecium** may have one pistil (**monocarpellary**) or many. When many pistils are fused it is **syncarpous** (e.g. Papaver, poppy); when free, **apocarpous** (e.g. Michelia). Each pistil has three parts: **stigma** (landing platform for pollen), **style** (a slender tube) and **ovary** (swollen base). Inside the ovary is a cavity, the **ovarian cavity (locule)**, and on the **placenta** sit the **ovules (megasporangia)**. The number of ovules varies hugely: one in wheat, paddy and mango; thousands in orchids and papaya.

### Structure of an ovule
- **Funicle** — stalk attaching the ovule to the placenta.
- **Hilum** — junction of ovule body and funicle.
- **Integuments** — one or two protective layers covering the ovule except at a small opening, the **micropyle**.
- **Chalaza** — the basal end, opposite the micropyle.
- **Nucellus** — mass of cells inside the integuments, rich in food.
- **Embryo sac (female gametophyte)** — lies in the nucellus. An ovule usually has a single embryo sac formed from one megaspore.

### Megasporogenesis
Near the micropyle, one cell of the nucellus differentiates into a **megaspore mother cell (MMC)** — large, dense cytoplasm, prominent nucleus. It divides by meiosis into **four megaspores**. In most flowering plants, three degenerate and only **one megaspore stays functional**. Development of an embryo sac from a single megaspore is called **monosporic development**.

### Building the 7-celled, 8-nucleate embryo sac
The functional megaspore's nucleus divides by **mitosis**, three times, *without immediate cell walls*:
- Division 1 → 2 nuclei, which move to opposite poles.
- Division 2 → 4 nuclei.
- Division 3 → 8 nuclei (4 at each pole).

Then walls form and the cells organise:
- **Micropylar end:** 3 cells = the **egg apparatus** — 2 **synergids** + 1 **egg cell**. The synergids have special cellular thickenings at the micropylar tip called the **filiform apparatus**, which guides the pollen tube in.
- **Chalazal end:** 3 **antipodal cells**.
- **Centre:** one large **central cell** with **two polar nuclei**.

So: **7 cells, 8 nuclei**. Remember this — it is asked every single year.

> **Did you know?** Because these divisions are free-nuclear (nuclei divide before walls form), for a short time the embryo sac is a single cell with eight nuclei floating in it.

sections.md:
**Pollination** is the transfer of pollen grains from the anther to the stigma of a pistil. Three kinds, based on the pollen source:

1. **Autogamy** — pollen reaches the stigma of the *same* flower. Needs anther dehiscence and stigma receptivity to be in sync and the two organs close together. Some plants have two types of flowers: **chasmogamous** (open, exposed anthers and stigma) and **cleistogamous** (never open) — e.g. Viola, Oxalis, Commelina. Cleistogamous flowers are invariably autogamous and assure seed set even without pollinators.
2. **Geitonogamy** — pollen from another flower of the *same plant*. Functionally cross-pollination (it needs an agent), but genetically similar to autogamy because the pollen comes from the same plant.
3. **Xenogamy** — pollen from a *different plant*. The only type that brings genetically different pollen.

### Agents of pollination
**Abiotic: wind and water.**
- *Wind (anemophily):* pollen light and non-sticky; well-exposed stamens; large, often feathery stigmas; flowers usually with a single ovule per ovary and many flowers packed into an inflorescence — the corn cob is a classic, its "tassels" are long styles and stigmas waving in the wind. Common in grasses.
- *Water (hydrophily):* rare, about 30 genera, mostly monocots — Vallisneria, Hydrilla, Zostera (sea grass). In Vallisneria, the female flower reaches the water surface on a long stalk and male flowers or pollen are released and carried passively by currents. In sea grasses, female flowers stay submerged and long ribbon-like pollen grains are carried inside the water. Pollen of water-pollinated plants is protected from wetting by a mucilaginous covering.
- Note: water hyacinth and water lily grow in water but are pollinated by insects or wind, like most land plants.

**Biotic: animals.** Bees, butterflies, flies, beetles, wasps, ants, moths, birds (sunbirds, hummingbirds), bats, even some primates and reptiles. Bees are the dominant pollinators. Insect-pollinated flowers are large, colourful, fragrant and rich in nectar; small flowers cluster into inflorescences to be noticed. Pollen is often sticky. Night-flowering plants pollinated by moths or bats are often white and strongly scented.

Rewards are nectar and pollen. Some species offer safe places to lay eggs. The **Amorphophallus** flower is about 6 feet tall. The famous partnership of the **yucca plant and a moth** is so close that neither can complete its life cycle without the other: the moth lays eggs in the ovary, the flower is pollinated, and the larvae eat some developing seeds.

Some visitors steal nectar or pollen without pollinating — **nectar robbers / pollen robbers**.

> **Did you know?** In some orchids (Ophrys), a petal looks and smells so much like a female bee that male bees try to mate with it — and get dusted with pollen in the process. This is called pseudocopulation.

check.q: Geitonogamy is functionally cross-pollination but genetically similar to autogamy because:
options: The pollen comes from the same plant
check.why: Although an agent carries pollen between flowers, both flowers are on the same plant, so the pollen is genetically identical to that plant's own.

sections.h: 5. Outbreeding devices and the pollen–pistil conversation
sections.md:
Repeated self-pollination leads to **inbreeding depression** — loss of vigour and fertility as harmful recessive alleles come together. Flowering plants have evolved several **outbreeding devices**:

- **Timing mismatch:** pollen released before the stigma is receptive (or vice versa).
- **Spatial separation:** anther and stigma placed at different positions so pollen cannot easily land on its own stigma.
- **Self-incompatibility:** a genetic mechanism where pollen from the same flower or plant is recognised and its germination or tube growth is blocked.
- **Unisexual flowers:** if male and female flowers are on the same plant (**monoecious**, e.g. castor, maize) autogamy is prevented but not geitonogamy. If on different plants (**dioecious**, e.g. papaya), both autogamy and geitonogamy are prevented.

### Pollen–pistil interaction
Landing on a stigma is not enough. The pistil **recognises** whether pollen is compatible — of the right species and, in self-incompatible species, not self. This is a chemical dialogue between molecules on the pollen and the pistil.

If compatible, the pollen grain **germinates**: a **pollen tube** emerges through a germ pore. The contents of the pollen grain move into the tube. The tube grows down through the stigma and style and reaches the ovary. In 2-celled pollen, the generative cell divides into two male gametes during this journey. The tube enters the ovule through the **micropyle**, then into one **synergid**, guided by the **filiform apparatus**.

If incompatible, the pistil stops it — at germination or tube growth.

These events, from pollen deposition to tube entry into the ovule, together are the **pollen–pistil interaction**.

### Plant breeders use this knowledge
In **artificial hybridisation**, a breeder wants only chosen pollen on a stigma:
- **Emasculation** — removing anthers from a bisexual flower bud *before* they dehisce, using forceps.
- **Bagging** — covering the emasculated flower with a butter-paper bag to keep out unwanted pollen.
- When the stigma becomes receptive, collected pollen from the desired male parent is dusted on, and the flower is re-bagged.
- For unisexual female flowers, emasculation is unnecessary; bagging alone is done.

> **Did you know?** You can watch pollen germinate at home: dust pea or balsam pollen onto a slide with a drop of sugar solution and look under a microscope after about 15–30 minutes.
keyTerms: Inbreeding depression — reduced vigour from continued self-breeding
Self-incompatibility — genetic block to self-pollen
Emasculation — removal of anthers before dehiscence
Bagging — covering flowers to prevent contamination

check.q: Which arrangement prevents BOTH autogamy and geitonogamy?
check.why: In dioecious species each plant bears only male or only female flowers, so pollen must come from a different plant.

sections.md:
After entering a synergid, the pollen tube releases the **two male gametes** into its cytoplasm. Now two fusions happen almost together:

1. **Syngamy:** one male gamete fuses with the **egg cell** → diploid **zygote (2n)**.
2. **Triple fusion:** the other male gamete fuses with the **two polar nuclei** in the central cell → triploid **primary endosperm nucleus, PEN (3n)**. The central cell now becomes the **primary endosperm cell (PEC)**.

Because two fusion events happen in one embryo sac, this is called **double fertilisation**, and it is unique to flowering plants.

| Fusion | Partners | Product | Ploidy |
|---|---|---|---|
| Syngamy | 1 male gamete + egg | Zygote → embryo | 2n |
| Triple fusion | 1 male gamete + 2 polar nuclei | PEN → endosperm | 3n |

A quick ploidy check: male gamete n + polar nucleus n + polar nucleus n = 3n. Male gamete n + egg n = 2n.

Why is this clever? The plant invests in a food tissue (endosperm) *only if* fertilisation actually happens. No fertilisation, no wasted food.

options: Two male gametes and the egg
One male gamete and two polar nuclei

sections.h: 7. After fertilisation: endosperm, embryo, seed and fruit
sections.md:
### Endosperm
Endosperm development comes **before** embryo development — sensible, because the embryo needs food. The PEC divides repeatedly to form a triploid **endosperm** full of reserve food.
- **Free-nuclear endosperm:** PEN divides many times without walls. The **coconut water** in a tender nut is free-nuclear endosperm made of thousands of nuclei; the white kernel around it is cellular endosperm.
- Later, walls form and the endosperm becomes **cellular**.
The endosperm may be fully eaten up by the embryo before seed maturity (pea, groundnut, beans — **non-albuminous/exalbuminous seeds**) or may persist (wheat, maize, barley, castor, coconut — **albuminous seeds**). In some seeds like black pepper and beet, remnants of the nucellus persist as **perisperm**.

### Embryo
The embryo develops at the micropylar end where the zygote sits. The zygote divides only after some endosperm has formed. It passes through **proembryo**, **globular** and **heart-shaped** stages to the mature embryo.

- **Dicot embryo:** an **embryonal axis** with **two cotyledons**. The part above the cotyledon attachment is the **epicotyl** ending in the **plumule** (shoot tip); below is the **hypocotyl** ending in the **radicle** (root tip), covered by a **root cap**.
- **Monocot embryo (e.g. grass family):** **one cotyledon**, called the **scutellum**, placed laterally. The radicle and root cap are enclosed in a sheath, the **coleorhiza**; the plumule and a few leaf primordia are in a hollow foliar sheath, the **coleoptile**.

### Seed
The seed is the final product of sexual reproduction — a **fertilised ovule**. It has seed coat(s), cotyledon(s) and an embryo axis. Integuments harden into the **seed coat**; the micropyle stays as a small pore through which oxygen and water enter during germination. As the seed matures, water content drops to about **10–15% moisture by mass**, metabolism slows and the embryo may enter **dormancy**.

Seeds can stay alive for astonishing periods. A lupine (Lupinus arcticus) seed dug from Arctic tundra germinated after an estimated **10,000 years** of dormancy. A **2,000-year-old** date palm seed (Phoenix dactylifera) recovered at King Herod's palace near the Dead Sea also germinated. Some orchid fruits hold thousands of tiny seeds; Orobanche and Striga parasitic species produce huge numbers too.

### Fruit
The **ovary develops into the fruit**, and the ovary wall becomes the **pericarp**. In mango and coconut the pericarp is fleshy or fibrous; in groundnut and mustard it is dry.
- **True fruit:** develops only from the ovary (most fruits).
- **False fruit:** other floral parts contribute — in apple, strawberry and cashew, the **thalamus** also contributes.
- **Parthenocarpic fruit:** develops without fertilisation, so it is seedless — banana is the classic example. Parthenocarpy can be induced with growth hormones.

### Why seeds are such a big deal
- Pollination and fertilisation are independent of water (unlike mosses and ferns).
- Seeds have adaptive strategies for dispersal to new habitats.
- Stored food nourishes the young seedling until it can photosynthesise.
- The hard coat protects the embryo.
- Being products of sexual reproduction, seeds carry new genetic combinations — the raw material of variation.
- Seeds are the basis of agriculture; dehydrated and dormant seeds can be stored for years as food and for sowing.

left.title: Dicot embryo (e.g. bean)
points: Radicle at tip of hypocotyl, with root cap

right.title: Monocot embryo (e.g. grass)
points: Radicle and root cap enclosed in coleorhiza
Epiblast may be present in some grasses

check.q: Coconut water in a tender coconut is:
check.why: The liquid is endosperm whose nuclei have divided without forming walls; the surrounding white kernel is the cellular part.

sections.h: 8. Apomixis and polyembryony: seeds without sex
sections.md:
Some species — certain grasses and members of the Asteraceae (sunflower family) — make seeds **without fertilisation**. This is **apomixis**, a form of asexual reproduction that mimics sexual reproduction.

How can it happen?
- A **diploid egg cell** forms without meiosis (no reduction division) and develops into an embryo without fertilisation.
- Or, in many varieties of **Citrus and mango**, some **nucellar cells** around the embryo sac divide, protrude into the embryo sac and develop into embryos.

When this happens, one seed can contain many embryos — **polyembryony**. Squeeze an orange seed and you may find several embryos of different sizes. The nucellar embryos are genetically identical to the mother; they are clones.

### Why breeders love apomixis
Farmers grow **hybrid seed** because hybrids give higher yields. But a hybrid's offspring segregate — the hybrid traits are lost in the next generation — so farmers must buy fresh hybrid seed every season, which is expensive. If hybrids could be made **apomictic**, the hybrid traits would stay fixed and farmers could save and reuse seed year after year. Scientists are actively studying the genes that control apomixis to transfer them into hybrid crops.

> **Did you know?** Apomixis is common in some wild grasses, which is why researchers look to them for the genetic switches that might one day give India's farmers cheaper, reusable hybrid seed.
keyTerms: Apomixis — seed formation without fertilisation
Polyembryony — more than one embryo in a seed
Nucellar embryony — embryos arising from nucellus cells

check.q: Why would apomictic hybrid seeds benefit farmers?
options: Hybrid traits would not segregate, so seed could be reused
They eliminate the need for pollinators only
check.why: Apomictic seeds are clones of the parent, so a hybrid's combination of traits is preserved in its seeds every year.

parts.md: Meera's grandmother had a red hibiscus by the gate in Kochi. Every morning at seven, a purple-rumped sunbird arrived, hung upside down, and pushed its curved beak deep into a flower. Meera, preparing for her board exams, started timing it with her phone: forty-two flowers in eleven minutes. "It's stealing," said her little brother. "It's working," said Meera. With a hand lens she showed him the yellow dust stuck on the bird's forehead feathers, right where the long staminal column of the hibiscus brushes past.

That evening she dusted some of the hibiscus pollen on a slide with a drop of sugar water. Twenty minutes later, under her school's microscope, thin tubes had begun to push out of the spiky grains. "Each one is trying to grow toward an egg it will never find on this slide," she wrote in her notebook. The next week, the flowers the sunbird had visited dropped their petals, and at the base of each, a tiny green capsule began to swell. The ovary was becoming a fruit. Inside, every ovule that a pollen tube had reached was turning into a seed — each carrying a little of the gate hibiscus and a little of some other hibiscus down the lane. Meera smiled: the bird had been a postman all along.

workedExamples.q: A plant has 2n = 24. Give the chromosome number in (a) a pollen grain cell (b) the egg (c) the zygote (d) the endosperm (e) the nucellus.
steps: n = 12, since gametes and gametophyte cells are haploid.
Pollen grain cells are male gametophyte cells: n = 12.
Zygote = male gamete n + egg n = 2n = 24.
Nucellus is sporophytic tissue of the mother plant: 2n = 24.

workedExamples.q: How many meiotic divisions are needed to produce 100 pollen grains and 100 functional megaspores (one embryo sac each)?
steps: One microspore mother cell gives 4 pollen grains in one meiosis, so 100 ÷ 4 = 25 meioses.
One megaspore mother cell gives 4 megaspores, but only one is functional, so each embryo sac needs 1 meiosis: 100 meioses.

workedExamples.q: An anther has 4 microsporangia; each has 50 pollen mother cells. How many pollen grains does one anther produce?
How many male gametes are needed to fertilise 50 ovules in an angiosperm? How many pollen grains?
steps: Each ovule undergoes double fertilisation, using 2 male gametes.
Each pollen grain produces 2 male gametes, so 100 ÷ 2 = 50 pollen grains.

summary: Flowers are the sites of sexual reproduction; stamens are male and pistils female organs.
A typical anther is bilobed, dithecous and has four microsporangia; the tapetum nourishes developing pollen.
Microsporogenesis: each pollen mother cell undergoes meiosis to form a tetrad of 4 microspores, which become pollen grains.
Pollen exine is made of sporopollenin, extremely resistant; germ pores lack it. Intine is cellulose and pectin.
Pollen is shed at 2-celled (vegetative + generative) stage in over 60% of angiosperms, else at 3-celled stage.
Ovule parts: funicle, hilum, integuments, micropyle, chalaza, nucellus, embryo sac.
Megaspore mother cell → meiosis → 4 megaspores; one functional (monosporic development).
Three mitotic divisions give the 7-celled, 8-nucleate embryo sac: egg apparatus (2 synergids + egg), 3 antipodals, central cell with 2 polar nuclei.
Pollination: autogamy, geitonogamy, xenogamy; agents are wind, water and animals.
Outbreeding devices: timing, position, self-incompatibility, unisexual (monoecious/dioecious) flowers.
Emasculation and bagging allow controlled crosses in breeding.
Double fertilisation: syngamy (zygote, 2n) + triple fusion (PEN, 3n) — unique to angiosperms.
Endosperm forms before the embryo; seeds may be albuminous or non-albuminous; perisperm is residual nucellus.
Ovule → seed, ovary → fruit, ovary wall → pericarp; false fruits include thalamus; parthenocarpic fruits are seedless.
Apomixis is seed formation without fertilisation; polyembryony is common in Citrus and mango.

glossary.d: Very resistant organic material of the pollen exine
Finger-like thickenings of synergids that guide the pollen tube
Flowers that never open; always self-pollinated
The single, lateral cotyledon of a grass embryo
Persistent remains of nucellus in a seed
Fruit formation without fertilisation

rd-school-c12-biology-a.ch02-human-repro.title: Human Reproduction
rd-school-c12-biology-a.ch02-human-repro.subtitle: From a single cell to a newborn's first cry — the biology of how every one of us began

sections.h: 1. Every one of us began as one cell
sections.md:
Here is a fact worth pausing on: every person reading this — every cricketer, every scientist, every grandparent — was once a single cell smaller than the full stop at the end of this sentence. Within about nine months that cell became trillions of organised cells with a beating heart, working kidneys and a brain.

Humans are **sexually reproducing** and **viviparous** (giving birth to young ones). The reproductive events follow a clear sequence that this chapter follows step by step:

1. **Gametogenesis** — formation of gametes: sperms in males, ova (eggs) in females.
2. **Insemination** — transfer of sperms into the female reproductive tract.
3. **Fertilisation** — fusion of a sperm with an ovum to form a **zygote**.
4. **Cleavage and blastocyst formation**, then **implantation** — attachment to the uterine wall.
5. **Gestation** — embryonic and foetal development.
6. **Parturition** — delivery of the baby.

Reproductive events begin after **puberty**. There are notable differences between the sexes: in males, sperm formation continues even in old age, while in females, ova formation ceases around the age of fifty years (**menopause**).

We will discuss these topics in the calm, factual language of a biology textbook. They are part of understanding the human body, just like digestion or breathing.
keyTerms: Viviparous — giving birth to live young
Gametogenesis — formation of gametes
Puberty — the stage when reproductive organs mature

sections.md:
The male reproductive system is located in the pelvis region. It includes a pair of **testes**, accessory ducts, glands and the external genitalia.

### Testes
The testes lie outside the abdominal cavity within a pouch called the **scrotum**. The scrotum keeps the testes about **2–2.5 °C lower** than normal internal body temperature — necessary for sperm formation. Each adult testis is oval, about 4–5 cm long and 2–3 cm wide.

Each testis has about **250 compartments** called **testicular lobules**. Each lobule contains **one to three highly coiled seminiferous tubules**, where sperms are made. Each tubule is lined by two types of cells:
- **Male germ cells (spermatogonia)** — undergo meiotic divisions to form sperms.
- **Sertoli cells** — provide nutrition to the germ cells.

In the spaces between tubules (**interstitial spaces**) lie **Leydig cells (interstitial cells)**, which synthesise and secrete testicular hormones called **androgens**, chiefly testosterone. Immunologically competent cells are also present there.

### Accessory ducts
Sperm travel along: seminiferous tubules → **rete testis** → **vasa efferentia** → **epididymis** (along the back surface of each testis) → **vas deferens** (ascends to the abdomen, loops over the urinary bladder) → joins the duct from the seminal vesicle to form the **ejaculatory duct** → **urethra**, which opens to the outside through the **urethral meatus**.

### Glands
The male accessory glands include paired **seminal vesicles**, a **prostate** and paired **bulbourethral glands**. Their secretions form the **seminal plasma**, which is rich in fructose, calcium and certain enzymes. Bulbourethral secretions also help in lubrication.

### External genitalia
The **penis** is made of special tissue that helps in erection to facilitate insemination. Its enlarged end is the **glans penis**, covered by a loose fold of skin called the **foreskin**.

sections.md:
The female reproductive system consists of a pair of **ovaries**, a pair of **oviducts**, the **uterus**, **cervix**, **vagina** and external genitalia in the pelvic region, along with the **mammary glands**.

### Ovaries
The primary female sex organs; they produce the **ovum** and several **steroid hormones (ovarian hormones)**. Each ovary is about 2–4 cm long and connected to the pelvic wall and uterus by ligaments. It is covered by a thin epithelium enclosing the **ovarian stroma**, which has an outer **cortex** and inner **medulla**.

### Oviducts (fallopian tubes)
Each is about 10–12 cm long, extending from the ovary to the uterus:
- **Infundibulum** — funnel-shaped part closest to the ovary, with finger-like **fimbriae** that help collect the ovum after ovulation.
- **Ampulla** — the wider part; fertilisation usually occurs at the **ampullary-isthmic junction**.
- **Isthmus** — the narrow last part joining the uterus.

### Uterus (womb)
Single, shaped like an inverted pear, supported by ligaments. It opens into the vagina through a narrow **cervix**; the cavity of the cervix is the **cervical canal**, which with the vagina forms the **birth canal**. The uterine wall has three layers:
- **Perimetrium** — outer thin membrane.
- **Myometrium** — middle, thick layer of smooth muscle; shows strong contractions during delivery.
- **Endometrium** — inner glandular layer lining the cavity; undergoes cyclical changes during the menstrual cycle.

### External genitalia and mammary glands
The external genitalia include the mons pubis, labia majora, labia minora, hymen and clitoris. The presence or absence of the hymen is **not** a reliable indicator of anything about a woman's history — it may be torn by a fall, exercise like cycling or horse-riding, or tampon use, and in some women it persists.

A functional **mammary gland** is characteristic of all female mammals. Each breast has glandular tissue divided into 15–20 **mammary lobes**, containing clusters of cells called **alveoli** that secrete milk. Milk is stored in the alveoli and flows through **mammary tubules → mammary duct → mammary ampulla → lactiferous duct** to the nipple.

sections.md:
### Spermatogenesis
Begins at puberty in the seminiferous tubules.
1. **Spermatogonia (2n, 46 chromosomes)** multiply by mitosis.
2. Some become **primary spermatocytes (2n)**, which undergo the first meiotic division.
3. Each forms two **secondary spermatocytes (n, 23 chromosomes)**.
4. These undergo the second meiotic division to form four **spermatids (n)**.
5. Spermatids transform into **spermatozoa (sperms)** — a process called **spermiogenesis**.
6. Sperm heads stay embedded in Sertoli cells and are finally released from the tubules — **spermiation**.

**Hormonal control:** At puberty, the hypothalamus increases secretion of **gonadotropin releasing hormone (GnRH)**. GnRH acts on the anterior pituitary to release **LH** and **FSH**. LH acts on Leydig cells → androgens, which stimulate spermatogenesis. FSH acts on Sertoli cells → factors that help spermiogenesis.

**Sperm structure:** a microscopic structure with a **head, neck, middle piece and tail**, covered by plasma membrane. The head has an elongated haploid nucleus capped by the **acrosome**, which carries enzymes that help fertilisation. The middle piece has numerous **mitochondria** producing energy for tail movement.

A human male ejaculates about **200 to 300 million sperms** per coitus. For normal fertility, at least **60%** should have normal shape and size, and at least **40%** must show vigorous motility. Sperms with seminal plasma together form **semen**.

### Oogenesis
It begins during **foetal development**, before birth! Millions of **oogonia** form in each foetal ovary; none are added after birth.
1. Oogonia start meiosis and get stuck in prophase-I as **primary oocytes**.
2. Each primary oocyte gets surrounded by a layer of granulosa cells → **primary follicle**. A large number degenerate from birth to puberty, so at puberty only about **60,000–80,000** primary follicles are left in each ovary.
3. Primary follicles gain more layers of granulosa cells and a theca → **secondary follicles**.
4. A fluid-filled cavity, the **antrum**, appears → **tertiary follicle**, with theca interna and theca externa.
5. The primary oocyte completes meiosis I inside the tertiary follicle — an **unequal division** producing a large haploid **secondary oocyte** and a tiny **first polar body**. The secondary oocyte keeps most of the cytoplasm.
6. The tertiary follicle becomes the mature **Graafian follicle**. The secondary oocyte forms a new membrane called the **zona pellucida**.
7. The Graafian follicle ruptures to release the secondary oocyte (ovum) — **ovulation**.

Meiosis II of the secondary oocyte is completed only if a sperm enters it.

sections.md:
The reproductive cycle in female primates (monkeys, apes, humans) is the **menstrual cycle**. The first menstruation, at puberty, is **menarche**. The cycle repeats on average every **28–29 days**. Its phases:

### 1. Menstrual phase (days 1–5, roughly 3–5 days)
The endometrial lining of the uterus and its blood vessels break down and flow out as menstrual blood. This happens only if the released ovum is not fertilised. **Lack of menstruation may indicate pregnancy**, but may also be caused by stress, poor health and other factors.

### 2. Follicular phase (proliferative phase)
Primary follicles grow into a fully mature Graafian follicle. Simultaneously the endometrium **regenerates by proliferation**. These changes are brought about by pituitary and ovarian hormones. LH and FSH rise gradually and stimulate follicle growth and **estrogen** secretion by the growing follicles.

### 3. Ovulation (around day 14)
LH and FSH reach a peak in the middle of the cycle. The rapid rise in LH, called the **LH surge**, induces rupture of the Graafian follicle and release of the ovum.

### 4. Luteal phase (secretory phase)
The remaining parts of the Graafian follicle transform into the **corpus luteum**, which secretes large amounts of **progesterone**. Progesterone is essential for **maintaining the endometrium**, needed for implantation of a fertilised ovum and other events of pregnancy. During pregnancy, all events of the menstrual cycle stop and there is no menstruation.

If fertilisation does not happen, the corpus luteum degenerates, progesterone falls, and the endometrium disintegrates — starting the next menstruation.

In humans, menstrual cycles cease around 50 years of age — **menopause**. Cyclic menstruation is an indicator of normal reproductive phase.

> **Did you know?** Menstrual hygiene is a health topic, not a taboo. Using clean sanitary products, changing them regularly and disposing of them safely matters for every girl's health and schooling.

sections.md:
During coitus, semen is released into the vagina (**insemination**). Motile sperms swim through the cervix, enter the uterus and reach the junction of the ampulla and isthmus of the oviduct. The ovum released by the ovary is also transported there. **Fertilisation can occur only if the ovum and sperms reach the ampullary-isthmic junction together.** That is why not all copulations lead to fertilisation and pregnancy.

### The process
- A sperm contacts the **zona pellucida** of the ovum, which induces changes in the membrane that **block entry of additional sperms** — ensuring only one sperm fertilises an ovum.
- Acrosome enzymes help the sperm penetrate the cytoplasm of the ovum through the zona pellucida and plasma membrane.
- Sperm entry triggers completion of **meiosis II** of the secondary oocyte, giving a second polar body and a haploid ovum (ootid).
- The haploid nucleus of the sperm and that of the ovum fuse → a **diploid zygote**.

### Who decides the sex of the baby?
Humans have the XY system. Females are XX; all ova carry an X. Males are XY; 50% of sperms carry X and 50% carry Y. If an X-sperm fertilises the ovum, the zygote is **XX (female)**; if a Y-sperm, the zygote is **XY (male)**. So **the sex of the baby is determined by the father's sperm**, not the mother — a crucial fact that undercuts any blame placed on women for the sex of a child.

### Cleavage and implantation
As the zygote moves through the isthmus toward the uterus, it undergoes **mitotic divisions called cleavage**, forming 2, 4, 8, 16 daughter cells called **blastomeres**. An embryo with 8–16 blastomeres is a **morula**. The morula continues to divide and becomes a **blastocyst** as it reaches the uterus.

In the blastocyst, blastomeres are arranged in an outer layer, the **trophoblast**, and an inner group of cells attached to it, the **inner cell mass**. The trophoblast attaches to the endometrium; the inner cell mass gets differentiated as the embryo. After attachment, uterine cells divide rapidly and cover the blastocyst; the blastocyst becomes embedded in the endometrium — **implantation**. This leads to pregnancy.

> **Did you know?** The inner cell mass contains **stem cells** that can give rise to all tissues and organs — which is why stem-cell research attracts so much interest.

options: The ovum, since it may carry X or Y

sections.md:
After implantation, finger-like projections called **chorionic villi** appear on the trophoblast. They are surrounded by uterine tissue and maternal blood. The chorionic villi and uterine tissue become interdigitated and together form a structural and functional unit between the developing embryo (foetus) and the mother — the **placenta**.

### Functions of the placenta
- Supplies **oxygen and nutrients** to the embryo.
- Removes **carbon dioxide and excretory/waste** materials from the embryo.
- Connected to the embryo through an **umbilical cord** that carries substances to and from the embryo.
- Acts as an **endocrine tissue**, producing **human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG)**, **human placental lactogen (hPL)**, estrogens, progestogens and others. In the later phase, the ovary secretes **relaxin**.

hCG, hPL and relaxin are produced in women *only during pregnancy*. Levels of other hormones like estrogens, progestogens, cortisol, prolactin and thyroxine also rise several-fold. These are essential for supporting foetal growth, metabolic changes in the mother and maintaining pregnancy. (Home pregnancy test kits detect hCG in urine.)

### Germ layers
After implantation, the inner cell mass differentiates into an outer layer **ectoderm** and an inner layer **endoderm**. A **mesoderm** soon appears between them. These three layers give rise to all tissues (organs) in adults.

### Milestones of development
| Time | Milestone |
|---|---|
| After one month | Embryo's **heart** is formed; first sign of growing foetus noticed by listening to heart sound with a stethoscope |
| End of second month | Limbs and digits develop |
| End of 12 weeks (first trimester) | Most major organ systems are formed; limbs and external genital organs well developed |
| Fifth month | First movements of the foetus; appearance of hair on the head |
| End of ~24 weeks (second trimester) | Body covered with fine hair, eyelids separate, eyelashes formed |
| End of nine months | Foetus fully developed and ready for delivery |

The average duration of human pregnancy (**gestation**) is about **9 months**.

check.q: Which hormone is produced only during pregnancy and is detected in pregnancy test kits?
check.why: Human chorionic gonadotropin is secreted by the placenta and is present only in pregnancy, so test kits look for it in urine.

sections.md:
Vigorous contractions of the uterus at the end of pregnancy cause expulsion/delivery of the foetus. This process of delivery is **parturition**.

Parturition is induced by a **complex neuroendocrine mechanism**. Signals originate from the **fully developed foetus and the placenta**, which induce mild uterine contractions called the **foetal ejection reflex**. This triggers release of **oxytocin** from the maternal pituitary. Oxytocin acts on the uterine muscle, causing stronger contractions, which in turn stimulate further oxytocin secretion. This **positive feedback** loop continues, leading to expulsion of the baby out of the uterus through the birth canal. Soon after, the placenta is also expelled.

### Lactation
The mammary glands undergo differentiation during pregnancy and start producing milk towards the end of pregnancy — **lactation**. This helps the mother feed the newborn.

The milk produced during the **initial few days of lactation** is called **colostrum**. It contains several **antibodies** absolutely essential to develop resistance for the newborn babies. Breastfeeding during the initial period of infant growth is recommended by doctors for bringing up a healthy baby.

> **Did you know?** Positive feedback loops are rare in the body; most hormonal systems use negative feedback to stay steady. Parturition is one of the few places where the body deliberately amplifies a signal until the job is done.
keyTerms: Foetal ejection reflex — mild contractions triggered by signals from foetus and placenta
Oxytocin — pituitary hormone causing strong uterine contractions
Colostrum — first milk, rich in antibodies

check.q: The hormonal loop during parturition is an example of:
check.why: Uterine contractions stimulate more oxytocin release, which causes stronger contractions — the signal amplifies itself.

workedExamples.q: How many sperms are formed from 25 primary spermatocytes, and how many ova from 25 primary oocytes?
steps: Each primary spermatocyte undergoes meiosis to form 4 spermatids → 4 sperms.
Each primary oocyte gives only 1 ovum (the rest are polar bodies).

workedExamples.q: Give the chromosome number in human: spermatogonium, primary spermatocyte, secondary spermatocyte, spermatid, first polar body, zygote.
steps: Primary spermatocyte: before meiosis I, still 46.
Secondary spermatocyte: after meiosis I, haploid = 23.
First polar body: product of meiosis I, 23.

workedExamples.q: A semen sample has 250 million sperms; 55% have normal shape and 45% are vigorously motile. Is this within the normal fertility criteria?
steps: Count criterion: 200–300 million — 250 million is fine.
Shape criterion: at least 60% normal — 55% is below.
Motility: at least 40% vigorous — 45% meets it.
workedExamples.answer: No — morphology (55%) falls short of the 60% normal-shape criterion, though count and motility are adequate.

summary: Human reproduction: gametogenesis → insemination → fertilisation → implantation → gestation → parturition.
Testes lie in the scrotum, 2–2.5 °C cooler than the body; each has ~250 lobules with 1–3 seminiferous tubules.
Sertoli cells nourish germ cells; Leydig cells secrete androgens.
Male duct path: rete testis → vasa efferentia → epididymis → vas deferens → ejaculatory duct → urethra.
Seminal plasma (from seminal vesicles, prostate, bulbourethral glands) is rich in fructose, calcium and enzymes.
Oviduct parts: infundibulum with fimbriae, ampulla, isthmus; uterine wall: perimetrium, myometrium, endometrium.
Spermatogenesis starts at puberty under GnRH → LH (Leydig cells) and FSH (Sertoli cells).
Oogenesis begins before birth; secondary oocyte is released at ovulation; meiosis II completes only after sperm entry.
Menstrual cycle (~28 days): menstrual, follicular, ovulatory (LH surge), luteal (corpus luteum → progesterone).
Fertilisation occurs at the ampullary-isthmic junction; zona pellucida changes block polyspermy.
The sperm determines the sex of the child (X or Y).
Cleavage → morula → blastocyst (trophoblast + inner cell mass) → implantation in the endometrium.
Placenta exchanges materials and secretes hCG, hPL, estrogens, progestogens; relaxin comes later from the ovary.
Parturition is driven by the foetal ejection reflex and oxytocin in a positive feedback loop.
Colostrum provides antibodies to the newborn.

sections.h: 9. Sectional view of a seminiferous tubule
sections.md:
The textbook asks you to *draw and label* a section through a seminiferous tubule. Picture a ring seen under a microscope.

- **Outside the ring:** the **interstitial spaces** with clusters of **Leydig (interstitial) cells**, small blood vessels and immunologically competent cells.
- **The wall:** a thin basement layer, then the **germinal epithelium**.
- **From the outside inward, the germ cells mature:** spermatogonia sit against the wall → primary spermatocytes → secondary spermatocytes → spermatids → spermatozoa, whose tails point into the **lumen** (the central cavity).
- **Sertoli cells** are tall cells stretching from the wall to the lumen; developing sperms are embedded in them and fed by them.

So the section is a map of time: the further a cell is from the wall, the later its stage. Labels to include: spermatogonium, primary spermatocyte, secondary spermatocyte, spermatid, sperm, Sertoli cell, Leydig cell, lumen.

sections.h: 10. Section of an ovary and the structure of a sperm
sections.md:
**Ovary section (diagrammatic).** A single drawing shows all stages around the cortex, as if travelling clockwise: primary follicles (oocyte with one layer of granulosa cells) → secondary follicle (many layers, theca forming) → tertiary follicle (fluid-filled **antrum**, theca interna and externa) → **Graafian follicle** (large antrum, secondary oocyte on a stalk of cells, zona pellucida) → **ovulation** (ruptured follicle releasing the oocyte) → **corpus luteum** (yellow body) → degenerating corpus luteum (corpus albicans, if no pregnancy). Blood vessels enter through the medulla.

**Structure of a sperm.**
| Part | Contents | Function |
|---|---|---|
| Head | Elongated haploid nucleus; acrosome cap | Carries paternal chromosomes; acrosome enzymes digest a path into the ovum |
| Neck | Centrioles | Links head and middle piece |
| Middle piece | Numerous mitochondria in a spiral | Supply energy (ATP) for swimming |
| Tail | Axial filament | Movement towards the ovum |

**Structure of the mature ovum/secondary oocyte at ovulation:** large haploid cell rich in cytoplasm, surrounded by the **zona pellucida** and, outside it, a layer of follicle cells called the **corona radiata**. The first polar body lies just beneath the zona.

fig.alt: Animated sperm with labelled parts and a waving tail.

check.q: The energy for sperm movement comes from:
check.why: Mitochondria in the middle piece produce ATP that powers the beating of the tail.

sections.md:
Many exam answers come down to knowing *which gland makes which hormone and what it does*.

| Hormone | Source | Main role |
|---|---|---|
| GnRH | Hypothalamus | Stimulates anterior pituitary to release LH and FSH |
| LH (male) | Anterior pituitary | Acts on Leydig cells → androgens |
| FSH (male) | Anterior pituitary | Acts on Sertoli cells → factors aiding spermiogenesis |
| Androgens (testosterone) | Leydig cells | Spermatogenesis, male secondary sexual characters |
| FSH (female) | Anterior pituitary | Follicle growth, estrogen secretion |
| LH (female) | Anterior pituitary | Mid-cycle surge → ovulation; forms corpus luteum |
| Estrogen | Growing follicles | Proliferation (regeneration) of endometrium |
| Progesterone | Corpus luteum (later placenta) | Maintains endometrium for implantation and pregnancy |
| hCG, hPL | Placenta | Maintain pregnancy, support foetal growth, maternal metabolism |
| Relaxin | Ovary (late pregnancy) | Helps in parturition by softening pelvic ligaments |
| Oxytocin | Posterior pituitary (maternal) | Strong uterine contractions; milk ejection |
| Prolactin | Anterior pituitary | Milk production |

**Two feedback types to remember.** Most of these hormones run on *negative feedback* (high testosterone damps GnRH). Parturition uses *positive feedback* (contractions → more oxytocin → stronger contractions).

check.q: Which hormone, produced by the corpus luteum, maintains the endometrium?
check.why: Progesterone from the corpus luteum keeps the endometrium thick and secretory, ready for implantation.

sections.h: 12. Exam traps and how to avoid them
sections.md:
1. **'The ovum is released at ovulation.'** Strictly, a *secondary oocyte* arrested in metaphase II is released. Meiosis II finishes only after sperm entry.
2. **Number of chromosomes vs. ploidy.** A primary spermatocyte is 2n (46) even though it has begun meiosis.
3. **'Hymen is proof of virginity.'** It is not. Biology says it may tear from sport or activity, or persist.
4. **Fertilisation site.** Ampullary-isthmic junction — *not* the uterus.
5. **Blastocyst parts.** Trophoblast attaches and later forms chorionic villi/placenta; inner cell mass forms the embryo.
6. **Ectoderm–endoderm–mesoderm.** Ectoderm and endoderm form first; mesoderm appears between them.
7. **Heart first.** The heart forms after one month; by 12 weeks most organ systems exist.
8. **Sex determination.** Father's sperm decides; the mother's ovum always contributes an X.
9. **Colostrum** is not 'impure' milk — it is the most protective milk a baby gets.
10. **Menstrual phase** is the *breakdown* of the endometrium; the follicular phase is its *rebuilding*.

> Did you know? Identical twins arise when one early embryo splits into two; non-identical (fraternal) twins come from two separate ova fertilised by two sperms in the same cycle.

check.q: Fraternal (non-identical) twins arise from:
options: One ovum and one sperm, embryo splits
Two ova fertilised by two sperms
One ovum fertilised by two sperms
check.why: Two separate ova released in the same cycle are each fertilised by a different sperm, giving genetically different twins.

workedExamples.q: A woman's cycle is 28 days and day 1 was 1 March. On roughly which day is ovulation expected, and when does the luteal phase end if there is no fertilisation?
steps: Ovulation is around day 14 → about 14 March.
Luteal phase runs from about day 15 to day 28 → ends about 28 March.
workedExamples.answer: Ovulation ≈ 14 March; luteal phase ends ≈ 28 March

workedExamples.q: How many meiotic divisions are needed to form 100 sperms, and 100 ova?
steps: One primary spermatocyte gives 4 sperms via 2 meiotic divisions (meiosis I and II).
100 sperms need 25 primary spermatocytes → 25 meiosis I + 50 meiosis II = 75 divisions.
Each ovum needs one primary oocyte: meiosis I (1) + meiosis II of secondary oocyte (1) = 2 per ovum (ignoring polar body division).
100 ova → 100 meiosis I + 100 meiosis II = 200 divisions.

summary: A seminiferous tubule section shows germ cells maturing from wall to lumen with Sertoli cells among them and Leydig cells outside.
An ovary section shows primary → secondary → tertiary → Graafian follicle → ovulation → corpus luteum.
Sperm: head (nucleus, acrosome), neck, middle piece (mitochondria), tail.
Secondary oocyte is surrounded by zona pellucida and corona radiata.
GnRH → LH and FSH; LH → Leydig cells/ovulation; FSH → Sertoli cells/follicle growth.
Progesterone maintains the endometrium; estrogen rebuilds it.
hCG, hPL and relaxin are made only during pregnancy.
Oxytocin drives parturition by positive feedback; prolactin makes milk.
Identical twins: one embryo splits; fraternal twins: two ova, two sperms.

rd-school-c12-biology-a.ch03-reproductiv.title: Reproductive Health
rd-school-c12-biology-a.ch03-reproductiv.subtitle: Why a nation's health begins with information, dignity and choice — population, contraception, STIs and infertility explained calmly

sections.md:
Imagine two villages. In the first, girls are married at fifteen, nobody talks about infections, and a mother walks 20 km to reach the nearest clinic. In the second, teenagers learn the facts in school, clinics offer counselling, and couples decide when to have children. Which village has healthier families? The answer is obvious — and it explains why reproductive health is a matter of public policy, not just private life.

The **World Health Organisation (WHO)** describes reproductive health as a total well-being in all aspects of reproduction — **physical, emotional, behavioural and social**. A society with people having physically and functionally normal reproductive organs and normal emotional and behavioural interactions in all sex-related aspects can be called reproductively healthy.

### India's journey
India was among the **first countries in the world** to start action plans and programmes at a national level to attain total reproductive health as a social goal. These programmes, called **family planning**, were initiated in **1951** and periodically assessed over the decades. Improved programmes covering wider reproduction-related areas are currently operating as **Reproductive and Child Health Care (RCH) programmes**.

Key strategies used:
- **Awareness** through audio-visual and print media, by government and non-government agencies.
- **Sex education in schools**, so young people get correct information and are discouraged from myths and misconceptions.
- Information on reproductive organs, adolescence, safe and hygienic sexual practices, sexually transmitted infections (STIs), AIDS etc.
- Educating couples and those in the marriageable age group about birth control options, care of pregnant mothers, post-natal care of mother and child, importance of breastfeeding, and **equal opportunities for the male and the female child**.
- Awareness of problems due to uncontrolled population growth and social evils like **sex abuse and sex-related crimes**.
- Building infrastructure, professional expertise and material support for medical assistance in pregnancy, delivery, STIs, abortions, contraception, menstrual problems and infertility.

### Legal and medical progress
- A **statutory ban on amniocentesis for sex determination**, to curb female foeticide. (Amniocentesis tests chromosomes in amniotic fluid to detect genetic disorders; misuse for sex selection is illegal.)
- **Massive child immunisation** programmes.
- Research on new, safer contraceptive methods; one example is the non-steroidal oral pill **Saheli**, developed by scientists at the Central Drug Research Institute (CDRI), Lucknow.

Better awareness, medically assisted deliveries and post-natal care have decreased **maternal and infant mortality rates**, increased the number of couples with small families, improved detection and care of STIs, and overall increased medical facilities for sex-related problems.

check.q: Why is amniocentesis banned for sex determination in India?
options: It is used to curb female foeticide
check.why: The statutory ban stops misuse of the test to identify and abort female foetuses, while its legitimate use for genetic disorders continues.

sections.md:
Better health facilities and living conditions led to an explosive impact on population growth. World population was around **2 billion (2000 million) in 1900** and rocketed to about **6 billion (6000 million) by 2000**, and over **7.2 billion in 2011**. India's population was approximately **350 million at independence**, crossed **1 billion in May 2000** and reached about **1.2 billion in 2011** — then about 1 in every 6 persons in the world was Indian.

### Why did it grow so fast?
- A rapid decline in **death rate**.
- A fall in **maternal mortality rate (MMR)** and **infant mortality rate (IMR)**.
- An increase in the number of people in the **reproducible age**.

The RCH programme helped bring the growth rate down, but only marginally at first. According to the 2011 census, the population growth rate was less than **2%**, i.e., 20 per 1000 per year — still a rate at which the population increases rapidly.

### Measures
- Motivating smaller families by using contraceptive methods. Slogans like *Hum Do Hamare Do* (we two, our two) were widely displayed; many young couples in urban areas adopted *one child norm*.
- Raising the **statutory marriageable age** to **18 years for females and 21 years for males**.
- Incentives for couples with small families.

### What makes an ideal contraceptive?
An ideal contraceptive should be **user-friendly, easily available, effective, reversible**, with **no or least side effects**, and should in no way interfere with sexual drive, desire or sexual act of the user.

> **Did you know?** Population growth slows with education. Wherever girls stay in school longer, the average age at marriage rises and families tend to be smaller — one reason education for girls is such a powerful public-health tool.

check.q: Which of these is NOT a property of an ideal contraceptive?
check.why: An ideal contraceptive must not interfere with sexual drive or the sexual act; all the other properties are desirable.

sections.md:
Contraceptive methods fall into several groups. This is educational information — a person choosing a method should always consult a qualified doctor.

### Natural / traditional methods
Based on avoiding chances of ovum and sperm meeting.
- **Periodic abstinence:** avoiding coitus from **day 10 to 17** of the menstrual cycle, when ovulation is expected; this is the fertile period.
- **Withdrawal (coitus interruptus):** the male partner withdraws before ejaculation.
- **Lactational amenorrhea:** absence of menstruation during intense lactation after delivery; ovulation and the cycle do not occur. Effective only up to a maximum of **six months** after parturition, and only while breastfeeding is full.
These have no side effects but high failure rates.

### Barrier methods
Prevent the physical meeting of ovum and sperm.
- **Condoms** — thin rubber/latex sheaths for the penis (male) or vagina and cervix (female). Popular brand: **Nirodh** for males. Their big advantage: they also **protect against STIs and AIDS**. They are disposable and can be self-inserted, giving privacy.
- **Diaphragms, cervical caps and vaults** — rubber barriers inserted into the female tract to cover the cervix during coitus; reusable. Often used with **spermicidal** creams, jellies and foams.

### Intra-uterine devices (IUDs)
Inserted by doctors or trained nurses into the uterus through the vagina.
- **Non-medicated IUDs** — e.g. Lippes loop.
- **Copper-releasing IUDs** — CuT, Cu7, Multiload 375. Copper ions suppress **sperm motility and fertilising capacity**.
- **Hormone-releasing IUDs** — Progestasert, LNG-20. Make the uterus unsuitable for implantation and the cervix hostile to sperms.
IUDs increase **phagocytosis of sperms** in the uterus. They are ideal for females who want to **delay pregnancy or space children**, and are one of the most widely accepted methods in India.

### Oral pills
Small doses of progestogens alone or progestogen–estrogen combinations taken daily for 21 days, starting within the first five days of the cycle. After a gap of 7 days (when menstruation occurs), the course repeats. Pills **inhibit ovulation and implantation**, and alter the quality of cervical mucus to prevent or slow entry of sperms. **Saheli** — the once-a-week non-steroidal pill from CDRI — has very few side effects and high contraceptive value.

### Injectables and implants
Progestogens alone or combined with estrogen can be given as injections or implants under the skin; they act like pills but work over a much longer period.

### Emergency contraception
Administering progestogens or progestogen–estrogen combinations, or IUDs, **within 72 hours of coitus** has been found very effective as emergency contraceptives — e.g., after rape or casual unprotected intercourse.

### Surgical methods (sterilisation)
Usually advised for a person who wants no more children; a **terminal**, generally irreversible method.
- **Vasectomy** (male): a small part of the vas deferens is removed or tied up through a small incision on the scrotum.
- **Tubectomy** (female): a small part of the fallopian tube is removed or tied up through a small incision in the abdomen or through the vagina.
They block gamete transport. Reversibility is very poor.

All methods have possible side effects for some users — nausea, abdominal pain, breakthrough bleeding, irregular bleeding — which is exactly why medical guidance matters.
