sections.md:
VBT says the metal uses **hybridised orbitals** (s, p, d) to accept electron pairs from ligands. Hybridisation decides shape:

| CN | Hybridisation | Shape |
|---|---|---|
| 4 | sp³ | tetrahedral |
| 4 | dsp² | square planar |
| 5 | sp³d | trigonal bipyramidal |
| 6 | sp³d² | octahedral (outer orbital) |
| 6 | d²sp³ | octahedral (inner orbital) |

**[Co(NH₃)₆]³⁺**: Co³⁺ is 3d⁶. NH₃ pairs up the six electrons into three 3d orbitals, leaving two 3d empty → **d²sp³**, inner-orbital (low-spin), **diamagnetic**.

**[CoF₆]³⁻**: F⁻ is weak and does not force pairing; four unpaired electrons remain; outer 4d orbitals are used → **sp³d²**, outer-orbital (high-spin), **paramagnetic**.

**[NiCl₄]²⁻**: Ni²⁺ 3d⁸, two unpaired; sp³ tetrahedral, paramagnetic.

**[Ni(CN)₄]²⁻**: CN⁻ forces pairing, one 3d orbital freed → dsp², square planar, diamagnetic.

**Magnetic data** test the theory: measured moments reveal unpaired electrons and thus which hybridisation occurs.

**Limitations of VBT**: involves assumptions; gives no quantitative interpretation of magnetic data; does not explain colour; does not distinguish strong and weak ligands; cannot predict exactly whether a 4-coordinate complex is tetrahedral or square planar; gives no quantitative thermodynamic or kinetic stabilities.

check.q: [Ni(CN)₄]²⁻ is
check.why: Strong-field CN⁻ pairs the two unpaired 3d electrons of Ni²⁺, freeing a d orbital for dsp² hybridisation.

sections.md:
CFT treats ligands as **point charges** (anions) or point dipoles (neutral molecules) and the metal–ligand bond as purely **ionic/electrostatic**. In a free ion the five d-orbitals are **degenerate**. Ligands approaching break this degeneracy — **crystal field splitting**.

**Octahedral field.** Ligands approach along the axes. Orbitals pointing at them (d_x²–y², d_z², the **e_g** set) are repelled more and rise; the three pointing between axes (d_xy, d_yz, d_xz, the **t₂g** set) fall. The energy gap is **Δ₀** (crystal field splitting energy). e_g lies +0.6Δ₀ above and t₂g –0.4Δ₀ below the average (barycentre).

**Spectrochemical series** (ligands in increasing field strength, from experiment):

I⁻ < Br⁻ < SCN⁻ < Cl⁻ < S²⁻ < F⁻ < OH⁻ < C₂O₄²⁻ < H₂O < NCS⁻ < edta⁴⁻ < NH₃ < en < CN⁻ < CO

**Filling d⁴ and beyond.** The 4th electron can either pair in t₂g (costing pairing energy P) or go up to e_g (costing Δ₀):
- **Δ₀ < P** (weak field): t₂g³e_g¹, **high-spin**.
- **Δ₀ > P** (strong field): t₂g⁴e_g⁰, **low-spin**.

**Tetrahedral field.** Splitting is inverted (e below, t₂ above) and smaller: **Δt = (4/9)Δ₀**. Pairing energy almost always exceeds Δt, so tetrahedral complexes are generally high-spin. (No g subscript because a tetrahedron lacks a centre of symmetry.)

**Colour.** A complex absorbs light of energy matching Δ and shows the complementary colour. [Ti(H₂O)₆]³⁺ (d¹) absorbs blue-green (≈ 498 nm) and appears violet. Remove water from CuSO₄·5H₂O and it turns white — no ligand field, no d–d transition. [Ni(H₂O)₆]²⁺ is green; adding en turns it blue/violet as Δ₀ increases. Without ligands there is no colour.

**Limitations**: treats ligands as point charges, so anionic ligands should split most — yet they are at the weak end. It ignores covalent character of bonding.

sections.md:
**Metal carbonyls** are homoleptic complexes with CO ligands: Ni(CO)₄ (tetrahedral), Fe(CO)₅ (trigonal bipyramidal), Cr(CO)₆ (octahedral), and Mn₂(CO)₁₀ and Co₂(CO)₈ (with metal–metal bonds; in Co₂(CO)₈ two CO groups also bridge).

The M–C bond has **both σ and π character — synergic bonding**:
1. **σ-bond**: CO donates its carbon lone pair into a vacant metal orbital.
2. **π back-bond**: a filled metal d-orbital donates electron density back into the vacant antibonding π* orbital of CO.

Each effect strengthens the other — hence 'synergic'. Back-donation strengthens M–C but weakens the C≡O bond slightly. This explains why CO, a neutral molecule, sits at the strong-field end of the spectrochemical series, and why metals in low oxidation states (0 here) form stable carbonyls.

check.q: Synergic bonding in metal carbonyls involves
options: σ donation from CO and π back-donation from metal
check.why: CO donates a lone pair to the metal (σ) while filled metal d orbitals push electrons back into CO's π* orbitals.

sections.md:
- **Analytical chemistry**: colour reactions and precipitates identify metals — Ni²⁺ with dimethylglyoxime (DMG) gives a red precipitate; Cu²⁺ with NH₃ gives deep blue; EDTA titrations estimate **hardness of water** (Ca²⁺, Mg²⁺ form stable EDTA complexes).
- **Metallurgy**: gold and silver are extracted as cyanide complexes [Au(CN)₂]⁻ and [Ag(CN)₂]⁻, then reduced by zinc. Nickel is purified by **Mond process** — impure Ni + CO → Ni(CO)₄, which decomposes on heating to pure Ni.
- **Biology**: chlorophyll (Mg), haemoglobin (Fe), vitamin B₁₂ cyanocobalamin (Co); many enzymes like carboxypeptidase A (Zn) and cytochromes (Fe).
- **Catalysis**: Wilkinson's catalyst [(Ph₃P)₃RhCl] for hydrogenation of alkenes.
- **Electroplating**: smooth, even coatings of Ag and Au from [Ag(CN)₂]⁻ and [Au(CN)₂]⁻ solutions.
- **Photography**: developed film is fixed by washing with hypo, which dissolves undecomposed AgBr as [Ag(S₂O₃)₂]³⁻.
- **Medicine**: EDTA treats lead poisoning; D-penicillamine and desferrioxamine B remove excess copper and iron (chelate therapy); **cisplatin** cis-[Pt(NH₃)₂Cl₂] inhibits tumour growth.

> Did you know? Only the *cis* isomer of [Pt(NH₃)₂Cl₂] is an anticancer drug; the trans isomer is not effective — geometry matters in medicine.

check.why: Nickel forms volatile Ni(CO)₄ with CO, which is then decomposed by heat to give pure nickel.

rd-school-c12-chemistry-a.ch05-coordinat.subtitle: Double salts, magnetism, colour, tetrahedral splitting and stability

sections.md:
Both form when two salts crystallise together in fixed ratios, but they behave differently in water.

- **Double salts** such as Mohr's salt FeSO₄·(NH₄)₂SO₄·6H₂O and potash alum KAl(SO₄)₂·12H₂O dissociate *completely* into simple ions. A solution of Mohr's salt gives all the tests of Fe²⁺, NH₄⁺ and SO₄²⁻.
- **Complexes** such as K₄[Fe(CN)₆] keep the complex ion intact. Its solution gives no test for Fe²⁺ or CN⁻, only for K⁺ and [Fe(CN)₆]⁴⁻.

Werner's conductivity and AgNO₃ precipitation experiments (part 1) used exactly this difference to count ionisable chlorides in CoCl₃·xNH₃.

check.q: Which gives a positive test for Fe²⁺ ions in solution?
check.why: Mohr's salt is a double salt that dissociates completely, releasing free Fe²⁺ ions.

sections.h: Magnetic properties and inner/outer orbital complexes
sections.md:
Magnetic moment tells us how many unpaired electrons the metal has, which in turn tells which orbitals are used.

- **[Fe(CN)₆]³⁻**: Fe³⁺ is d⁵. CN⁻ is strong, electrons pair into three 3d orbitals leaving one unpaired; d²sp³ hybrid, **inner orbital**, low spin, paramagnetic (≈1.73 BM).
- **[FeF₆]³⁻**: F⁻ is weak; five unpaired electrons remain; sp³d² using 4d orbitals, **outer orbital**, high spin (≈5.92 BM).
- **[Ni(CN)₄]²⁻**: Ni²⁺ d⁸; pairing gives dsp², square planar, diamagnetic.
- **[NiCl₄]²⁻**: no pairing; sp³, tetrahedral, two unpaired, paramagnetic.

**Limitations of VBT**: it involves assumptions; gives no quantitative interpretation of magnetic data; does not explain colour; cannot reliably predict tetrahedral vs square planar for 4-coordinate complexes; does not distinguish weak and strong ligands.

check.q: [Ni(CN)₄]²⁻ is:
check.why: Strong-field CN⁻ forces pairing of Ni²⁺'s d⁸ electrons, freeing one 3d orbital for dsp² hybridisation, giving square planar and no unpaired electrons.

sections.h: Spectrochemical series and the pairing decision
sections.md:
Ligands are arranged by the size of splitting Δ they cause (the **spectrochemical series**, found experimentally):

I⁻ < Br⁻ < SCN⁻ < Cl⁻ < S²⁻ < F⁻ < OH⁻ < C₂O₄²⁻ < H₂O < NCS⁻ < edta⁴⁻ < NH₃ < en < CN⁻ < CO

For d⁴ ions in an octahedral field, the fourth electron has a choice:
- If **Δ₀ < P** (pairing energy), it enters e_g → t₂g³e_g¹, **high spin** (weak field ligand).
- If **Δ₀ > P**, it pairs in t₂g → t₂g⁴e_g⁰, **low spin** (strong field ligand).

**Tetrahedral splitting**: the order is reversed — e lower, t₂ higher — and Δt ≈ (4/9)Δ₀. Because Δt is so small, pairing is usually unfavourable and **low-spin tetrahedral complexes are rarely observed**.

sections.md:
When white light falls on a complex, an electron jumps from t₂g to e_g (a **d–d transition**) by absorbing light of energy Δ₀. We see the **complementary colour**.

- [Ti(H₂O)₆]³⁺ (d¹) absorbs blue-green and looks **violet**.
- Remove water from [Ti(H₂O)₆]Cl₃ by heating and it becomes colourless — no ligand field, no splitting.
- Anhydrous CuSO₄ is white; CuSO₄·5H₂O is blue.
- [Ni(H₂O)₆]²⁺ is green; adding ethane-1,2-diamine step by step gives blue and then violet as Δ increases.

d⁰ (Sc³⁺, Ti⁴⁺) and d¹⁰ (Zn²⁺, Cu⁺) ions cannot have d–d transitions and are usually colourless.

**Limitations of CFT**: it treats ligands as point charges, yet anionic ligands should then give the biggest splitting — they actually lie at the weak end of the series; it also ignores covalent character of bonding.

check.q: Why is anhydrous CuSO₄ white while CuSO₄·5H₂O is blue?
options: Water ligands cause d-orbital splitting allowing d–d transitions
check.why: Without water ligands there is no crystal-field splitting in the visible range, so no visible light is absorbed.

sections.md:
The stability of a complex in solution is measured by its **formation (stability) constant**. For M + 4L ⇌ ML₄ the overall constant β₄ = [ML₄]/[M][L]⁴, and β₄ = K₁K₂K₃K₄ (stepwise constants). A large β means a very stable complex; the instability constant is 1/β.

Stability increases with: higher charge density of the metal ion, more basic ligands, and **chelation** — polydentate ligands like en and EDTA form rings and give far more stable complexes than an equivalent number of monodentate ligands (the chelate effect).

check.q: For a complex formed in four steps, the overall stability constant β₄ equals:
check.why: Overall equilibrium is the sum of stepwise reactions, so its constant is the product of stepwise constants.

rd-school-c12-chemistry-b.ch06-haloalkan.title: Haloalkanes and Haloarenes
rd-school-c12-chemistry-b.ch06-haloalkan.subtitle: From chloroform in old operation theatres to DDT on cotton fields — carbon meets the halogens

sections.h: 1. Introduction: when a halogen replaces hydrogen
sections.md:
Replace a hydrogen atom of an alkane by a halogen and you get a **haloalkane (alkyl halide)**, R–X. Replace one on an aromatic ring and you get a **haloarene (aryl halide)**, Ar–X. In haloalkanes the halogen sits on an sp³ carbon; in haloarenes on an sp² carbon of the ring.

They matter everywhere: chloramphenicol (an antibiotic from soil microbes) treats typhoid; our thyroid makes **thyroxine**, an iodine-containing hormone whose deficiency causes goitre (hence iodised salt); chloroquine fights malaria; halothane was used as an anaesthetic; Teflon and PVC are polymers of halogen compounds. Some, like CFCs and DDT, have caused environmental harm — which this chapter discusses at the end.

The NCERT chapter runs: classification → nomenclature → nature of C–X bond → preparation of haloalkanes and haloarenes → physical properties → chemical reactions (nucleophilic substitution with SN1/SN2 and stereochemistry, elimination, reaction with metals; reactions of haloarenes) → polyhalogen compounds.

check.q: In a haloarene the halogen is attached to
options: an sp² carbon of an aromatic ring
a carbon next to a double bond
check.why: Aryl halides have X bonded directly to a ring carbon, which is sp² hybridised.

sections.md:
**On the number of halogen atoms**: mono-, di-, tri-, poly-haloalkanes/arenes (CH₃Cl, CH₂Cl₂, CHCl₃…).

**Compounds with sp³ C–X bond:**
- **Alkyl halides** R–X, classified by the carbon bearing X as **primary (1°)**, **secondary (2°)** or **tertiary (3°)** — e.g. CH₃CH₂Br (1°), (CH₃)₂CHBr (2°), (CH₃)₃CBr (3°).
- **Allylic halides**: X on an sp³ carbon next to a C=C (CH₂=CH–CH₂–X).
- **Benzylic halides**: X on an sp³ carbon next to an aromatic ring (C₆H₅CH₂X); can be 1°, 2°, 3°.

**Compounds with sp² C–X bond:**
- **Vinylic halides**: X on a carbon of a C=C (CH₂=CH–X).
- **Aryl halides**: X on a ring carbon (C₆H₅X).

**Dihalides**: **geminal** (both X on the same carbon, alkylidene halides, CH₃CHCl₂) and **vicinal** (on adjacent carbons, alkylene dihalides, CH₂Cl–CH₂Cl).

sections.h: 3. Nomenclature and the nature of the C–X bond
sections.md:
**Common names**: alkyl group + halide (methyl chloride, isopropyl bromide, tert-butyl chloride). **IUPAC**: halogen as a prefix on the parent chain (2-bromobutane, 1-chloro-2-methylpropane). For arenes: chlorobenzene; disubstituted arenes use 1,2 / 1,3 / 1,4 (common: ortho, meta, para): 1,4-dichlorobenzene = p-dichlorobenzene. Common names of polyhalo compounds: CH₂Cl₂ methylene chloride, CHCl₃ chloroform, CHI₃ iodoform, CCl₄ carbon tetrachloride; C₆H₅CH₂Cl benzyl chloride; CH₂=CHCl vinyl chloride; CH₂=CHCH₂Br allyl bromide.

**Nature of the C–X bond.** Halogens are more electronegative than carbon, so the bond is **polar**: Cδ+–Xδ–. Down the group, the halogen gets bigger, so **bond length increases** (C–F 139 pm < C–Cl 178 < C–Br 193 < C–I 214) and **bond enthalpy decreases** (C–F 452 > C–Cl 351 > C–Br 293 > C–I 234 kJ/mol). Dipole moments: CH₃Cl (1.860 D) is slightly higher than CH₃F (1.847 D) — the C–F bond is shorter, offsetting fluorine's higher charge — then CH₃Br 1.830 and CH₃I 1.636 D.

check.q: Which C–X bond is the weakest?
check.why: Iodine is the largest halogen, giving the longest bond and the lowest bond enthalpy (≈234 kJ/mol).

sections.md:
**Haloalkanes from alcohols** (most common): replace –OH.
- With concentrated HX: R–OH + HCl (with ZnCl₂, the *Groves process*) → R–Cl + H₂O. Reactivity of alcohols: 3° > 2° > 1°. Tertiary alcohols react with conc. HCl even at room temperature. HBr and HI work directly (HI from NaI + H₃PO₄).
- With phosphorus halides: 3R–OH + PCl₃ → 3R–Cl + H₃PO₃; R–OH + PCl₅ → R–Cl + POCl₃ + HCl. Red P with Br₂ or I₂ makes PBr₃/PI₃ in situ.
- With **thionyl chloride** (best method): R–OH + SOCl₂ → R–Cl + SO₂↑ + HCl↑ — both by-products are gases, leaving pure product.

Phenols *cannot* be converted to aryl halides this way because the C–O bond in phenol has partial double-bond character.

**From hydrocarbons:**
- *Free-radical halogenation* of alkanes (Cl₂, UV light or heat) gives mixtures of isomers — e.g. butane → 1-chlorobutane + 2-chlorobutane — so it is of limited lab use.
- *Electrophilic substitution* of arenes: benzene + Cl₂ with Lewis acid (FeCl₃, Fe) in the dark → chlorobenzene; toluene gives o- and p-chlorotoluene. Iodination needs an oxidant (HIO₃/HNO₃) to remove HI; fluorination is too violent.
- *Sandmeyer reaction*: aniline + NaNO₂/HCl at 273–278 K → benzenediazonium chloride; then CuCl/HCl or CuBr/HBr → chloro/bromobenzene. KI gives iodobenzene directly.
- *Addition to alkenes*: HX adds by **Markovnikov's rule** (propene + HBr → 2-bromopropane); with peroxide, HBr adds anti-Markovnikov (1-bromopropane). Br₂ in CCl₄ adds across C=C giving vicinal dibromide — the reddish-brown colour disappears (test for unsaturation).

**Halogen exchange:**
- *Finkelstein reaction*: R–Cl/Br + NaI (dry acetone) → R–I + NaCl/NaBr (NaCl and NaBr precipitate, driving it forward by Le Chatelier's principle).
- *Swarts reaction*: R–Br + AgF / Hg₂F₂ / CoF₂ / SbF₃ → R–F.

check.q: Why is thionyl chloride preferred for making alkyl chlorides from alcohols?
options: Its by-products SO₂ and HCl are gases and escape, leaving pure product
check.why: Since SO₂ and HCl escape as gases, the alkyl chloride is obtained almost pure.

sections.md:
Pure haloalkanes are colourless, but bromides and iodides turn coloured on exposure to light. Many volatile halogen compounds have a sweet smell.

**Boiling points**: higher than hydrocarbons of similar mass because of greater polarity and molecular mass → stronger dipole–dipole and van der Waals forces.
- For the same alkyl group: RI > RBr > RCl > RF (bigger, more polarisable).
- For isomers, b.p. decreases with branching: 1-bromobutane (375 K) > 2-bromobutane (364 K) > 2-bromo-2-methylpropane (346 K) — branched molecules are more spherical with less surface contact.
- CH₃F, CH₃Cl, CH₃Br, C₂H₅Cl are gases at room temperature.

**Melting points of isomeric dihalobenzenes**: para isomers melt highest because their symmetry lets them pack well in the crystal lattice (p-dichlorobenzene 323 K vs o- 256 K, m- 249 K). Boiling points of o, m, p isomers are nearly the same.

**Density**: increases with number of carbons, number of halogen atoms and atomic mass of halogen; bromo-, iodo- and polychloro- compounds are denser than water.

**Solubility**: only very slightly soluble in water — energy needed to break hydrogen bonds between water molecules is not compensated by the weaker attraction with R–X. They dissolve well in organic solvents.

check.q: Which isomer has the lowest boiling point?
check.why: Increased branching makes the molecule more compact, reducing surface area and van der Waals attractions.

sections.md:
Because the carbon of C–X is δ+, **nucleophiles** (electron-rich species) attack it and the halide leaves:

Nu⁻ + R–X → R–Nu + X⁻

| Reagent | Nucleophile | Product |
|---|---|---|
| NaOH/KOH (aq) | OH⁻ | alcohol ROH |
| H₂O | H₂O | alcohol |
| NaOR′ | R′O⁻ | ether (Williamson synthesis) |
| NaI | I⁻ | alkyl iodide |
| NH₃ | NH₃ | primary amine |
| KCN | CN⁻ (C-attack) | nitrile RCN |
| AgCN | Ag–C≡N (N-attack) | isonitrile RNC |
| KNO₂ | O–N=O (O-attack) | alkyl nitrite R–O–N=O |
| AgNO₂ | Ag–O–N=O (N-attack) | nitroalkane R–NO₂ |
| R′COOAg | R′COO⁻ | ester |
| LiAlH₄ | H⁻ | hydrocarbon RH |
| R′⁻M⁺ | R′⁻ | alkane RR′ |

KCN is mainly ionic and attacks through carbon (C–C bond more stable), while AgCN is covalent so only nitrogen's lone pair is free — giving isocyanides. CN⁻ and NO₂⁻ are **ambident nucleophiles**.

**SN2 (bimolecular)**: rate = k[RX][Nu⁻] — second order. One step: the nucleophile attacks from the **back side** (opposite to X), the carbon passes through a five-coordinate transition state, and the configuration turns inside out like an umbrella in a storm — **Walden inversion**. Hughes and Ingold proposed it (1937). Steric hindrance matters: reactivity **CH₃X > 1° > 2° > 3°**. Tertiary halides hardly react by SN2.

**SN1 (unimolecular)**: rate = k[RX] — first order, common in polar protic solvents (water, alcohol, acetic acid). Step 1 (slow): C–X breaks to form a **carbocation**. Step 2 (fast): nucleophile attacks the planar carbocation. Reactivity follows carbocation stability: **3° > 2° > 1° > CH₃X**. Example: (CH₃)₃CBr + OH⁻ → (CH₃)₃COH + Br⁻. Allylic and benzylic halides react readily by SN1 because their carbocations are resonance-stabilised.

For a given alkyl group, reactivity: **R–I > R–Br > R–Cl >> R–F** (weakest bond, best leaving group) in both mechanisms.

check.why: Methyl bromide has the least crowded carbon, so the nucleophile can reach the back side most easily.

sections.md:
**Plane-polarised light** vibrates in a single plane (from a Nicol prism). Some compounds rotate this plane — **optically active**. Measured in a **polarimeter**. Rotation to the right (clockwise) = **dextrorotatory (d or +)**; to the left = **laevorotatory (l or –)**.

**Molecular asymmetry, chirality.** Louis Pasteur (1848) separated two kinds of tartrate crystals that were mirror images. van't Hoff and Le Bel (1874) linked optical activity to a carbon bearing **four different groups** — an **asymmetric (chiral) centre (stereocentre)**. A chiral molecule is not superimposable on its mirror image, like your left and right hands. Butan-2-ol is chiral; propan-2-ol is not (two identical CH₃ groups).

**Enantiomers**: non-superimposable mirror-image pairs; identical physical properties except the direction of rotation of light. A 50:50 mixture is a **racemic mixture** (dl or ±) with zero rotation — the rotations cancel. Converting an enantiomer into a racemic mixture is **racemisation**.

**Retention and inversion.** **Retention** keeps the spatial arrangement of bonds around the stereocentre; **inversion** produces the opposite arrangement.
- **SN2** on an optically active halide gives **complete inversion** — e.g. (–)-2-bromooctane + OH⁻ → (+)-octan-2-ol.
- **SN1** on an optically active halide gives **racemisation** (often with some excess inversion), because the planar carbocation can be attacked from either face.

> Did you know? Many drugs are sold as single enantiomers because the mirror form can be inactive or even harmful.

sections.md:
**β-Elimination (dehydrohalogenation).** Heating a haloalkane with **alcoholic KOH** removes H from the β-carbon and X from the α-carbon, forming an alkene. When more than one alkene is possible, **Zaitsev's (Saytzeff's) rule** says the more substituted alkene (more alkyl groups on the double-bond carbons) is the major product: 2-bromobutane → but-2-ene (≈81%) + but-1-ene (≈19%).

**Substitution vs elimination.** A base/nucleophile can either pull off a proton (elimination) or attack carbon (substitution). Primary halides favour SN2; tertiary favour elimination with strong bases; bulky bases and high temperature favour elimination.

**Reaction with metals.**
- **Grignard reagent**: R–X + Mg in **dry ether** → RMgX (Victor Grignard, Nobel 1912). The C–Mg bond is highly polar and carbon is nucleophilic. Grignard reagents react with any proton source — water, alcohols, amines — to give hydrocarbons: RMgX + H₂O → RH + Mg(OH)X. Hence they must be kept dry.
- **Wurtz reaction**: 2R–X + 2Na (dry ether) → R–R + 2NaX — doubles the carbon chain.

check.q: 2-Bromobutane with alcoholic KOH gives mainly
check.why: By Zaitsev's rule the more substituted alkene, but-2-ene, is the major elimination product.

sections.md:
**Low reactivity towards nucleophilic substitution**, because:
1. **Resonance**: the lone pair on Cl is delocalised into the ring, giving C–Cl partial double-bond character — harder to break.
2. **sp² carbon**: more s-character, holds electrons tighter; C–Cl in chlorobenzene (169 pm) is shorter than in CH₃Cl (177 pm).
3. **Phenyl cation** is unstable (not resonance-stabilised), so SN1 is ruled out.
4. **Repulsion**: the electron-rich ring repels the incoming nucleophile; back-side attack is blocked by the ring.

**Forcing conditions**: Dow's process — chlorobenzene + NaOH at 623 K and 300 atm → phenol. **Electron-withdrawing groups** (–NO₂) at ortho/para positions make substitution easy: p-nitrochlorobenzene reacts at 443 K; 2,4-dinitro at 368 K; 2,4,6-trinitro with warm water. They stabilise the negative intermediate by resonance; a meta –NO₂ has no such effect.

**Electrophilic substitution**: halogen is slightly **deactivating** (–I effect) but **ortho, para-directing** (resonance raises electron density at o and p). Reactions are slower than benzene:
- Halogenation (Cl₂/FeCl₃) → 1,2- and 1,4-dichlorobenzene (para major).
- Nitration (conc. HNO₃ + H₂SO₄) → o- and p-chloronitrobenzene.
- Sulphonation (conc. H₂SO₄) → o- and p-chlorobenzenesulphonic acid.
- Friedel–Crafts alkylation (CH₃Cl/AlCl₃) and acylation (CH₃COCl/AlCl₃) → o- and p- products.

**With metals**: **Wurtz–Fittig reaction**: ArX + RX + 2Na (dry ether) → Ar–R (alkylarene). **Fittig reaction**: 2ArX + 2Na → Ar–Ar (diphenyl).

sections.md:
- **Dichloromethane (CH₂Cl₂)**: solvent for paint removal, propellant in aerosols, metal cleaning. Can harm the central nervous system; low levels cause slight hearing and vision impairment, dizziness; direct contact burns skin and eyes.
- **Trichloromethane (chloroform, CHCl₃)**: solvent for fats, alkaloids, iodine; used to make Freon refrigerant R-22. Once a general anaesthetic, now replaced by safer ones. Prolonged breathing affects the central nervous system and can damage liver and kidneys. In air and light it is slowly oxidised to poisonous **phosgene** (COCl₂), so it is stored in dark coloured bottles filled to the brim.
- **Triiodomethane (iodoform, CHI₃)**: was an antiseptic — the effect comes from liberated iodine, not iodoform itself; its unpleasant smell led to its replacement.
- **Tetrachloromethane (CCl₄)**: used to make refrigerants and aerosol propellants, and in pharmaceuticals; once used in dry cleaning and fire extinguishers. Exposure causes liver cancer risk, dizziness, nausea; it depletes the ozone layer when released.
- **Freons (CFCs)**, e.g. CCl₂F₂ (Freon-12): stable, non-toxic, non-flammable — used in aerosols, refrigerators and ACs. In the stratosphere, UV breaks them into chlorine free radicals that destroy ozone. The Montreal Protocol (1987) phased them out.
- **DDT** (p,p′-dichlorodiphenyltrichloroethane): first chlorinated insecticide; synthesised in 1873, its insecticidal action found by Paul Müller (Nobel 1948). Helped control malaria and typhus mosquitoes and lice. But it is not biodegradable, accumulates in fatty tissues and moves up food chains, harming fish and birds (thin eggshells). Many countries banned it; in India its use is now restricted.

check.q: Chloroform is stored in dark bottles filled to the top because
options: it is oxidised by air in light to poisonous phosgene
check.why: Light and oxygen convert CHCl₃ to COCl₂ (phosgene), so air and light are excluded.

summary: Haloalkanes have X on sp³ carbon; haloarenes on sp² ring carbon.
Classified as 1°/2°/3°, allylic, benzylic, vinylic, aryl; dihalides are geminal or vicinal.
C–X is polar; bond length increases and bond strength decreases from F to I.
Made from alcohols (HX/ZnCl₂, PX₃, PCl₅, SOCl₂), alkenes (Markovnikov), halogen exchange (Finkelstein, Swarts).
Haloarenes from benzene + X₂/FeX₃ or via diazonium salts (Sandmeyer).
B.p.: RI > RBr > RCl > RF; falls with branching; para dihalobenzene has highest m.p.
SN2: one step, second order, inversion; CH₃X > 1° > 2° > 3°.
SN1: carbocation, first order, racemisation; 3° > 2° > 1°.
KCN gives nitriles; AgCN gives isonitriles; KNO₂ nitrites; AgNO₂ nitroalkanes.
Chiral centre = four different groups; enantiomers rotate light oppositely; racemic mixture shows zero rotation.
Alcoholic KOH causes β-elimination following Zaitsev's rule.
Grignard reagents (RMgX) need dry ether; Wurtz, Wurtz–Fittig and Fittig reactions join carbon chains.
Haloarenes resist nucleophilic substitution; –NO₂ at o/p activates; halogen is o/p-directing but deactivating.
CHCl₃, CCl₄, freons and DDT are useful but have health/environmental hazards.
